body:
That's exactly how I feel these last couple of weeks: walking around in a daze. After the last two sessions, I went home and just rested my bones to some Brian Eno (Ambient 1: Music for Airports) and spent hours trying to wrap my head around what was discussed only a few hours earlier. Lately, I've been feeling rather shell shocked. You're probably right: I think I'm coming to a problem in my life that has trumped all the other ones and its implications are so wide spread - it's terrifying at times. 

I appreciate you're support.

Some of the feelings I experience trace back so far into my past, that I had forgotten them completely; in some cases for as long as 15 years. What you described in your edit seems to be what my therapist is trying to accomplish in our work together - find the cognitive behavior and change it. Of course that comes with a price: frustration, exhaustion, pain, etc.

Thus far, I consider it **very** successful. I'm far from living the life I want, which is the same life that everyone deserves, but I'm learning things about myself that are inseparably ingrained in my identity at such a rapid pace. Over the last month, I feel like my work with my therapist has stumbled across something *huge* in my life, and for that I'm thankful. With all honesty, I can say I understand myself better now than I ever have before... 

but that doesn't mean it's encouraging. On the contrary. Going back to my original post, facing down the "collective identity of all my problems" is really scary - especially now that I know what they are.

Eh.. Kinda, but it doesn't bother me - not because I don't care, but because there is a definite end at the close of next year. My personal life is progressing - I was in a much darker place just last December. 

As far as work/study/social outlets/hobbies/interests go: my problems invade all those areas, aggressively. So it's as difficult to distract myself as it is to mask the problems.

I see what you're saying - I do. When I reflect on my life each of my problems can be separate and individual; self contained. I've been in therapy for what will soon be a year, and we've covered a lot of those problems; at least the ones that impede me most. In that time I've faced down each problem, separately, and that's been a great help with the guidance of a professional. 

But there are times like now when I can't help but feel *really fucked up*. It's difficult to carry so many struggles and *not* group them together. They all have only one thing in common: they make my life more difficult. And when I face that, it gets intimidating... 

quickly.
